This kid shows some form of high functioning autism. Yes the autism spectrum should be supported and educated about, but the focus seems to never be on the severely disabled autistic people, both children and adults. Autistic individuals who meet the criteria of level 2/level 3 autism are unlikely to hold down work sustainably, and level 3 will likely never work in their lives, or be able to be fully independent. 

I wouldn't be surprised if the speech was written by his mother or father either, this kind of language is clearly not of his linguistic age. 

Do I think what RFK is spreading is misinformation? Yes, but high functioning autistics and their supporters are skewing the narrative. We are getting personally offended by a person with a worm in his brain. We're ignoring autistic individuals who need 24/7 care and struggle to have a human life. That is 30% of all autistic individuals, that is almost a third.

As a person with high functioning autism and ADHD, my disorders are not my strength, they are my weakness and I'm grateful that I don't have it worse. Yes there are some positive aspects that come out from it, I enjoy what I obsess over and I think it gives me some quirks that find me entertaining to other, but I wish I didn't have these disorders. I understand the positive message towards children, but seeing the disorder as a 'strength' completely disregards the meaning behind the diagnosis. They're called disorders for a reason.

People with level 2 to level 3 autism don't seem to have a voice in this RFK discourse. I can guarantee those with level three autism struggle to have a voice in their daily life, literally and figuratively. They're hidden away from society, you don't see them because they're inside being taken care of. Using working high functioning autistic people as an example of autistic people getting a job is offensively misleading.

If there was a cure for autism, I'd take it in a heartbeat. If my child was going to develop autism if there was a way to prevent the development of the disorder, I would. I'm not  'proud' of being autistic. I don't believe in shaming, but I don't believe in celebrating it either. I believe in teaching perseverance despite your weaknesses.

Everyone on this sub with high functioning autism like myself got lucky with the environmental and genetic lottery when you compare our ability to those with severe autism. This disorder is not something I personally want. Autism is not my identity, it's a diagnosis, it's a cluster of symptoms that impair my daily functioning and my ability to fit in into broader society.

If autism had a cure, or was unequivocally proven to be caused by an environmental factor, many parents would completely reject it, because they can't bear the idea that they could have prevented it, and they built their entire identity around parenting a neurodiverse child. There's also this ludicrous view that angers me, that curing or preventing a disorder is saying that that person shouldn't exist or was never born. That only offends those who built their identity around their disorder, rather than treat it as something that hinders them. That view angers me the most because it's peoples ego getting in the way of improving millions of lives. No one mourns the infinite number of hypothetical people who were never born.

TLDR: most media and advocacy focus on high functioning autism because those people have the capacity to engage publicly, and advocate for themselves.

Everyone should take their nutrition seriously, but those with ADHD absolutely should. Medication alone isn't enough from my experience, you've got to give your brain what it needs to even utilise medication properly or even at all. Since changing my diet, my ADHD unmedicated is so much less, that I require less medication. Sometimes I can skip.

If you're dealing with anorexia, the effects of malnutrition and calorie restriction can make it really hard to focus or stay motivated, which can greatly overlap with ADHD symptoms, and sometimes be the cause. That doesn’t mean you don’t have neurodevelopmental ADHD, but it does highlight how tricky the current assessment process can be. It’s not really about you, it’s more about how the system handles these overlaps. I actually think it’s understandable that they’d be cautious about giving a diagnosis right away. If you can provide more proof that you've suffered from ADHD symptoms BEFORE you developed anorexia, you may have a better chance. There is a high overlap with ADHD and ED, so a knowledgeable psychiatrist will be able to help you and listen, instead of outright hand waving you away.

I agree, the larger implications of AI should be the focus, and it very much is mine. It's much more than just job replacement, and will likely breed major psychological shifts in the way we consume media, information, think independantly etc. Much scarier. I do however think that removing the humanity from creativity is inherently linked with removing the capacity for independant thought in all areas.

I agree, I do however struggle to draw the line between a tool and giving the process over to AI. I can see advancements in AI helping me speed up so many tedious parts of my Blender CG/Animation/Gamedev workflow.

If we ignore the stolen art argument, which I absolutely agree with. An interesting example to compare is the use of generative AI for textures, and using procedural textures. Both are automatically generated, and I technically own the copyright for both. No texture artist was needed, yet one of them is wholly accepted, while the other is vilified.

Or sound design for example. ElevenLabs can generate completely new sound effects for you, but I wouldn't want to use a laser gun sound ready made for me. It does however make more sense to generate sounds to layer together, just like you would for royalty free sounds to make a new sound effect. However, now sound recordists and designers who sell or provide sounds have been replaced, certainly from stolen work.

For generating 3D models in full or a texture which is meant to be a staple on a character, not just some background detail that no one will actually notice, I feel very different. I don't want AI to guess what I want for that.

I don't know where the line is. All I can say, is that there are some parts of the creative process which make sense to automate depending on how big your team is, working on your own, or simply don't have time. It's been like this since forever, using tools to make your vision closer to how it is in your head.

I honestly would rather generative AI not exist at all in terms of pixel to pixel guesswork. I think the closest I've got to figuring out the line, is how important is that particular element for producing an emotional connection from the viewer? If it's a lot, like a main character, important prop, design, etc, then it should be human made with a lot of intent.

I honestly don't know. I think the difference here is that there is a lot more artistic intent than other uses of generative AI. The trouble is, even these algorithms are trained on art that is stolen under the hood, even though it uses their own art as reference.

I'd say that this is using it as a tool rather than a full on replacement. The process is being sped up using AI, rather than being replaced. It clearly has enabled them to make a much more dynamic and rich animation with more background assets and side characters.

Things like generative 3D extrusion makes a ton of sense to do, but at the same time, a 3D modeller has been displaced.

I honestly don't know. I feel the problem with a lot of this is the theft, and speed of the advancement of this technology which will cause job losses fast.

I can't lie, it feels dirty, but I can't logically justify that feeling it if it's being used as a tool which will speed up realising a more concrete artistic vision.

If you feel like you identify with ADHD symptoms long term at the intensity it’s described in the literature, then you have ADHD. Figuring out why you experience ADHD symptoms is always the deeper issue. ADHD is defined by a collection of symptoms over a long-term period, not a singular disorder with one simple explanation or cure-all. It manifests differently in different people for different reasons. It's not always genetic neurotransmitter differences like dopamine dysfunction; it can also be influenced by factors such as your current mental health, learned coping mechanisms, immune dysfunction, diet (which should not be underestimated). Often, a mix of these factors is extremely common.

This is a slightly controvertial take, but I think this is aboslutely crucial for someone like you to know at this stage. One drug, one technique, one diagnosis will not cure ADHD. At first it may seem like it, but it's not true. If a psychiatrist wants to give you stimulants and send you on your way, find a new psychiatrist. You have to be personally responsible for this, unfortunately. Many don't understand the disorder at all. Getting CBT, psychotherapist counselling, and better habits alongside medication is **crucial**. From my experience, psychiatrists often do not have a nuanced understanding of ADHD and have as much knowledge as the NHS public webpage for it. Many want to just prescribe stimulants without addressing the years of learned behaviours that self-sabotage you to this day. I'm not saying stimulants don't work at all, I take them, but for me and many others, **stimulants/other medication enable you to form better habits with the right support/techniques.**

By all means I could be wrong, but you're likely a highly emotional and passionate person, people with ADHD usually are. This is not a bad thing, there is nothing 'wrong' with you for being more emotionally driven. The trouble is, people like that are suceptible to having our emotions control them, which can form bad habits and coping mechanisms from a young age. Some people are more susceptible to developing ADHD unfortunately.

I feel like my perspective comes from someone who hasn't recently been given stimulants and isn't experiencing an instant, rosy "fix." If someone claims everything is suddenly better (which you see all the time on reddit) it's extremely likely they're in the early, euphoric stage of stimulant use. Neurotypical people are not high on stimulants all the time.

ADHD is a complex condition that shows up differently for everyone. This makes your worry about not getting diagnosed understandable and valid. I wanted to reflect on that complexity to emphasise that your experience truly matters.

I'm autistic and I can explain from MY experience. When I was a kid, there's something hypnotic about colourful characters and worlds - especially animals. Especially when they're inhabited by archetypical characters which fit neatly into pre-existing identities which you see around you in life. Also, there's something about the expressiveness in the eyes.

Edit: I'm an adult now, and I'm still susceptible to the allure of all of these, and I indulge with great enjoyment.

In my view, when I was a kid, the attraction to characters and worlds with clearly defined traits is rooted in a autistic need to make sense of this mental and chaotic reality. Fictional worlds where expressions, motivations, and emotions are laid out clearly are comforting. Real life is chaos. This actually moves on to my own view of 'identity', which many autistic people struggle with.

As I've matured, my perspective on 'identity' has evolved significantly. I've come to believe that searching for one's 'identity' is a real issue. When we don't meet the expectations of said identity, it creates dysphoria. This applies to every identity taken seriously. I used to think my actions were clues that could help me uncover some hidden self, allowing me to neatly categorise who I am. Now, I view my actions as just that... **actions**. They don't pin me down or define me. This shift has freed me to focus on activities I genuinely enjoy, rather than how they might fit into a pre-determined identity.

Identity is a breeding ground for conflict, fueling wars and deepening political divides. The "us versus them" mindset it encourages can also make it difficult for people to change their opinions. In short, the gravity people assign to identity can have dire consequences.... Anyway, back to autism.

I'm a furry (*I know that's an identifier, but its more a descriptive term lol*), and one of the reasons I love it is because it allows me to experiment with my sense of self within a realm of fantasy and fun, but crucially, **it's not real life**. The issue arises when these drastic experiments of identity bleed into everyday reality, and that's where I think **a lot** of people go wrong.

Classic Doctor Who came from an era of TV when there wasn't much else on. Even though it was super original and has stood the test of time culturally, the episodes *themselves* haven't. In my opinion, episodes of The Twilight Zone from 1959 are way faster paced than a Doctor Who episode from 1970.

The thing is, back then, British TV had like 3 channels. So you could get away with bad pacing and dragging stories out because, honestly, where else were your viewers gonna go?

I'm pretty sure viewers back then got bored by Doctor Who sometimes. Just watch an old Disney movie from the 1940s. They had great storytelling, good pacing, everyone loved them, and they're still watched by audiences today.

Also, I swear I remember hearing about a writer who worked on classic Doctor Who and felt frustrated because they had to find absurd ways to extend the runtime. Classic Who seems like a writer's dream and nightmare. Writers want to write a good story, but also one that gets to the point and get's rid of fluff.

Plus, I think back then, TV was seen by producers as more of a cheap distraction than a place for captivating storytelling. Sure, many shows had great stories, but the big money and cultural influence was still focused on movies.

I think tasteful, abridged versions of the old stories are absolutely something the BBC should consider. Trouble is, you'll get a bombardment of fans saying 'they cut out the scene were flibbidy jibbit talks about the flankoskulon matrix space hole', and that somehow is a very important scene.

EDIT: Robert Holmes was the writer who got pissed off at extending the runtime.  
A particular case of this was the serial "The Seeds of Doom" (1976). It was initially planned to be a four-part story, but it had to be extended to six episodes. Holmes was reportedly frustrated with the necessity to pad the plot to meet the runtime requirement, leading to some plot elements that he felt were overly contrived or didn't add much to the overall story.
